title: The Houston Apartment Build and Building Up Houston
goal: I can find equivalent fractions, simplify a fraction in one step with the GCF, convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers, and build an informative paragraph with a topic sentence, details, transitions and a concluding sentence.

card.desc: You help Amara's crew at a Houston apartment build: you show that tile patterns like 3/8 and 9/24 are equivalent, simplify floor-plan fractions in one step with the GCF (30/42 = 5/7), and convert pipe and steel-bar lengths between improper fractions and mixed numbers (19/4 = 4 3/4). Then you learn how an informative paragraph is built: a topic sentence, supporting details, transitions and a concluding sentence (Pathways Week 12). It is your first lesson back in January, and you start by presenting your Winter Games Record Book.

win: Every fraction in simplest form and every paragraph built floor by floor. Amara's building is ready for inspection, and you are ready for the Winter Games!

slides.title: The Houston Apartment Build and Building Up Houston
slides.text: Amara is helping her aunt's crew build a six-story apartment building in Houston, Texas. Tile patterns, floor plans, pipes and steel bars: every job is a fraction job. Today you learn to rename fractions, simplify them in one step, and convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers. Then you learn how a strong informative paragraph is built, one floor at a time.

notes.do: Before class: check his Lesson 6 Show What You Know score and his Pathways Week 11 Math and Reading scores (Formspree). Set out grid paper, a blue colored pencil, three highlighters, 10 index cards, the whiteboard and a marker. Math runs 9:30–10:05 (35 min); reading runs 10:05–10:30 (25 min).
notes.say: Two jobs today. First 35 minutes: fractions at the apartment build. Last 25 minutes: how writers build a paragraph. This is our last lesson of the year, so we finish by opening your Winter Games.
notes.ask: What do you think a construction crew measures in parts of a foot?
notes.listen: Pipes, tiles, boards, steel bars, windows. Any real example is fine.

slides.title: Three hallways
slides.text: Diego tiles three hallways. All three have the same length and width. Hallway A: 3 of 8 big tiles are blue. Hallway B: 6 of 16 medium tiles are blue. Hallway C: 9 of 24 small tiles are blue.

visual.sub: which hallway has the most blue floor?

prompts: Hallway C has the most blue tiles. Does it have the most blue FLOOR? Why or why not?
How are 3 and 8 connected to 6 and 16? To 9 and 24?
If a fourth hallway had 32 tiles, how many would be blue to match?
starters: I think … because the tiles are …
It would need … blue tiles, because …

notes.do: 2 to 3 minutes. Let him argue it out before slide 5 shows the picture. Write his three fractions on the whiteboard.
notes.ask: If you cut every tile in Hallway A in half, how many tiles would there be? How many blue?
notes.listen: 16 tiles and 6 blue: that is Hallway B. More tiles does not mean more floor; the tiles are smaller. For 32 tiles: 12 blue (3/8 × 4/4).

slides.title: Lessons 3, 4 and 6, then today
slides.text: Paper first, then type.

items.q: Lesson 6 skill: the greatest common factor (GCF) of 24 and 36 is ____.
items.why: Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. The greatest one in both lists is 12.
items.no: List the factors of each number in pairs. Find the biggest number in BOTH lists.

items.q: Lesson 4 skill: 2.4 × 3.5 = ____
items.why: Estimate: 2 × 4 = 8. 24 × 35 = 840. 2 decimal places → 8.40 = 8.4.
items.no: Multiply without the decimal points, then count the decimal places in BOTH factors.

items.q: Lesson 3 skill: 1/6 + 5/12 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: 12 is a multiple of 6, so the common denominator is 12. 1/6 = 2/12. 2/12 + 5/12 = 7/12.
items.no: Rename 1/6 in twelfths, then add only the numerators.

items.q: New today: 6/6, 9/9 and 25/25 are all equal to ____.
items.why: Any number (except 0) over itself is 1 whole: 6 sixths, 9 ninths, 25 twenty-fifths.
items.no: 6 slices of a pizza cut into 6 slices is how much pizza?

notes.do: He answers out loud, writes on paper, then types. If the Lesson 6 score was under 85, spend 2 extra minutes listing factor pairs for 24 and 36 on the whiteboard; today needs the GCF.
notes.say: Today the GCF from Lesson 6 becomes a power tool. And remember: any number over itself is 1.
notes.ask: Why is 25/25 the same as 1?
notes.listen: 25 parts out of 25 is all of it, one whole. That idea is why equivalent fractions work.

slides.title: Math words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word, the meaning and the example out loud.

words.meaning: A fraction whose numerator is equal to or bigger than its denominator. It is 1 whole or more.
words.example: 19/4 is an improper fraction: 19 fourths is more than 1 whole foot.

words.meaning: To rename a fraction with smaller numbers by dividing the numerator and the denominator by the same number.
words.example: Simplify 30/42: divide both by 6 to get 5/7.

words.meaning: To change a number into a different form that has the same value.
words.example: Convert 19/4 to a mixed number: 4 3/4.

words.meaning: A fraction with 1 as its numerator.
words.example: Each short pipe is 1/6 foot long. 1/6 is a unit fraction.

notes.do: He reads each card aloud, then covers it and says the meaning in his own words. He writes each word on the front of an index card.
notes.say: Pathways Week 12 asks for improper fraction by name. Simplify and convert are the two jobs we do all day.
notes.ask: What is the difference between an improper fraction and a mixed number?
notes.listen: 19/4 is improper (top bigger than bottom); 4 3/4 is a mixed number (a whole number with a fraction beside it). Same amount, two ways to write it.

steps.text: Equal blue floor. 3/8, 6/16 and 9/24 cover the same part of the hallway, so they are equivalent.
A → B: every tile is cut in 2. Twice as many tiles (8 → 16) and twice as many blue (3 → 6). 3/8 × 2/2 = 6/16.
Why it works: 2/2 = 1, 3/3 = 1, any n/n = 1. Multiplying by 1 never changes the amount. A → C: 3/8 × 3/3 = 9/24.
Going back: divide by n/n. 9/24 ÷ 3/3 = 3/8. Diego glues 3 small tiles back into 1 big tile.
Never add! Add 1 to the top and the bottom of 3/8 and you get 4/9. 4/9 is almost half the hallway, so it is MORE blue than 3/8. Not equal.

slides.tip: Same number, top and bottom. Multiply or divide. Never add.

notes.do: Hands-on: on grid paper he draws Hallway A as 8 boxes, each 2 squares wide, and colors 3 blue. Under it he draws Hallway B the same length as 16 boxes, 1 square each, and colors 6. The blue ends line up.
notes.say: An equivalent fraction is the same amount cut into a different number of pieces.
notes.ask: What do you multiply 3/8 by to get a denominator of 40?
notes.listen: 5/5, because 8 × 5 = 40, so 3/8 = 15/40. If he says “add 32,” go back to the tiles: adding makes a different amount.

slides.title: Equivalent fractions
slides.text: Find what the denominator (or numerator) was multiplied by. Do the same to the other number.

items.q: 4/9 = ____/36 Type the missing numerator.
items.why: 9 × 4 = 36, so multiply the numerator by 4 too: 4 × 4 = 16. 4/9 = 16/36.
items.no: What do you multiply 9 by to get 36? Multiply the numerator by that same number.

items.q: 5/6 = 30/____ Type the missing denominator.
items.why: 5 × 6 = 30, so multiply the denominator by 6 too: 6 × 6 = 36. 5/6 = 30/36.
items.no: This time the numerator changed. What do you multiply 5 by to get 30? Do the same to the denominator.

items.q: Which fraction is NOT equivalent to 6/10?
items.why: 6/10 ÷ 2/2 = 3/5, 6/10 × 2/2 = 12/20, and 3/5 × 3/3 = 9/15: all equal. 7/11 came from ADDING 1 to the top and bottom, so it is a different amount.
no: 6/10 ÷ 2/2 = 3/5. It IS equivalent.
6/10 × 2/2 = 12/20. It IS equivalent.
3/5 × 3/3 = 9/15, and 3/5 = 6/10. It IS equivalent.

notes.do: He writes the multiplier (×4/4, ×6/6) next to each one before he types.
notes.ask: For 5/6 = 30/____, why does the denominator change by 6?
notes.listen: 5 × 6 = 30 on top, so 6 × 6 = 36 on the bottom. Watch for 31 (adding 25 to the bottom) or 30 typed as the denominator.

steps.text: Small steps work, slowly. 30/42 ÷ 2/2 = 15/21. Then 15/21 ÷ 3/3 = 5/7. Two steps, and it is easy to stop too early.
One step with the GCF (Lesson 6). Factors of 30: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. Factors of 42: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 21, 42. The greatest common factor is 6.
Check: 5 and 7 share no factor except 1, so we are done: 5/7 is in simplest form. The grid agrees: 5 of its 7 columns are gold.
To simplify is to divide. The amount never changes. Only the numbers get smaller.

slides.tip: Simplest form: the numerator and the denominator share no factor except 1.

notes.do: On the whiteboard he lists the factor pairs of 30 and 42 (1 × 30, 2 × 15, 3 × 10, 5 × 6) and circles the GCF. Then he checks the grid: 5 gold columns out of 7.
notes.say: Dividing by the GCF gets you to simplest form in ONE step. Any smaller common factor means more steps.
notes.ask: If you divided 30/42 by 3/3 first, would you be done?
notes.listen: No: 10/14, and 10 and 14 still share 2. That is why the GCF is the fastest.

slides.title: Simplify it
slides.text: List the factors on paper. Divide by the GCF.

items.q: Simplify in one step with the GCF: 24/32 = ____
items.no: Find the greatest common factor of the numerator and the denominator. Divide BOTH by it. Then check: do the new numbers share any factor except 1?

items.q: To simplify 36/54 in ONE step, divide the numerator and the denominator by:
no: 9 is a common factor, but 36/54 ÷ 9/9 = 4/6, and 4/6 still simplifies. 9 is not the GREATEST.
12 is a factor of 36, but not of 54 (54 ÷ 12 is not a whole number).
6 gives 6/9, which still simplifies. Look for a greater common factor.

items.q: Which fraction can NOT be simplified any further?
items.why: 9 = 3 × 3 and 14 = 2 × 7. They share no factor except 1, so 9/14 is in simplest form.
no: 6 and 16 are both even: they share 2. 6/16 = 3/8.

notes.do: Hands off. He lists factors on paper for each one.
notes.ask: How do you know 9/14 can't be simplified?
notes.listen: The factors of 9 are 1, 3, 9 and the factors of 14 are 1, 2, 7, 14. Only 1 is in both. Watch for 3/4 typed as 6/8 or 12/16 (stopped early).

steps.text: Improper → mixed: divide. 19 ÷ 4 = 4 R3. The quotient, 4, is the whole feet. The remainder, 3, is the fourths left over. 19/4 = 4 3/4.
Check it on the line: 4 wholes = 16 fourths, plus 3 more fourths = 19 fourths. ✅
Mixed → improper: Darnell needs a steel bar 3 5/6 feet long, and his chart counts sixths. 3 wholes = 3 × 6 = 18 sixths. Add the 5: 18 + 5 = 23. 3 5/6 = 23/6.
The denominator never changes when you convert. Fourths stay fourths and sixths stay sixths.
Simplest form counts here too. 26/4 = 6 R2 = 6 2/4, and 2/4 = 1/2, so 26/4 = 6 1/2. Always look at the fraction part.

slides.tip: Improper → mixed: divide, and the remainder goes over the same denominator. Mixed → improper: whole × denominator, plus the numerator.

notes.do: Hands-on: on grid paper he draws a number line from 0 to 5 with 4 squares for each foot, then hops 19 squares from 0 and reads where he lands (4 and 3 more squares).
notes.say: Converting uses your Lesson 2 division: the remainder finally has a home. It becomes the numerator.
notes.ask: Why does 3 5/6 have 18 sixths before you add the 5?
notes.listen: Each whole foot is 6 sixths, and there are 3 wholes: 3 × 6 = 18.

slides.title: Convert it
slides.text: Type a mixed number with a space: 4 3/5.

items.q: Change it to a mixed number: 27/5 = ____
items.why: 27 ÷ 5 = 5 R2. The quotient 5 is the whole number. The remainder 2 is the new numerator, and the denominator stays 5. 5 2/5
items.no: Divide the numerator by the denominator. The quotient is the whole number, the remainder is the new numerator, and the denominator stays the same. Type a space between the whole number and the fraction.

items.q: Change it to an improper fraction: 6 2/7 = ____/7 Type the numerator.
items.why: 6 wholes = 6 × 7 = 42 sevenths. Add the 2 more: 42 + 2 = 44. 6 2/7 = 44/7.
items.no: Multiply the whole number by the denominator first (6 × 7), then add the numerator. The denominator stays 7.

items.q: Which is 34/8 as a mixed number in simplest form?
items.why: 34 ÷ 8 = 4 R2, so 34/8 = 4 2/8. Simplify the fraction part: 2/8 = 1/4. 4 1/4
no: 4 2/8 is the right amount, but 2/8 is not in simplest form. Divide both by 2.
The quotient and the remainder got switched. 34 ÷ 8 = 4 R2: the 4 is the whole number.
2/8 is not 1/2. Divide 2 and 8 by 2: 1/4.

notes.do: He says the division out loud for each one (27 ÷ 5 = 5 R2) before he types.
notes.ask: For 6 2/7, what two steps did you do?
notes.listen: 6 × 7 = 42, then 42 + 2 = 44, so 44/7. Watch for 6 × 2 = 12 (multiplying by the numerator) or 15 (adding 6 + 2 + 7).

slides.title: Two steps for Ms. Okafor
slides.text: Ms. Okafor, the project engineer, needs two numbers for her report.

steps.text: The lobby: 54 tiles cover the floor. 36 are blue, and every other tile is white. Step 1: 54 − 36 = 18 white tiles, so 18/54 of the floor is white.
Step 2: simplify with the GCF. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. 54 ÷ 18 = 3, so 18 is a factor of 54 too. GCF = 18. 18/54 = 1/3 of the floor is white.
The pipe: Mr. Nguyen lines up 21 short pipes, each 1/6 foot long (a unit fraction). 21 pieces of 1/6 = 21/6 feet.
Convert, then simplify: 21 ÷ 6 = 3 R3, so 21/6 = 3 3/6. 3/6 = 1/2. The line is 3 1/2 feet.
Read the question twice: blue or white? Improper fraction or mixed number? Simplest form?

slides.tip: Underline what the question asks for before you start.

notes.do: He works both on paper and underlines “white” and “mixed number” in the question before he starts.
notes.say: Pathways' real-world and Boss questions are all two steps like these.
notes.ask: What answer do you get if you forget step 1 in the lobby problem?
notes.listen: 36/54 = 2/3, the BLUE part. The question asked for white.

slides.title: Two-step jobs
slides.text: Underline what the question asks for. Paper first.

items.q: A laundry room floor is covered with 45 tiles. 27 of them are gray, and every other tile is white. What fraction of the tiles are white? Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Step 1: 45 − 27 = 18 white tiles, so 18/45. Step 2: the GCF of 18 and 45 is 9. 18 ÷ 9 = 2 and 45 ÷ 9 = 5. 2/5
items.no: Two steps. First subtract to find how many are white. Then write that number over 45 and divide both by the GCF.

items.q: Mr. Nguyen joins 26 pieces of pipe into one straight line. Every piece is 1/8 foot long. How long is the line? Type a mixed number in simplest form.
items.why: 26 pieces of 1/8 = 26/8 feet. 26 ÷ 8 = 3 R2, so 26/8 = 3 2/8. 2/8 simplifies to 1/4 (divide both by 2). 3 1/4 feet
items.no: Write it as an improper fraction first (26/8). Then divide to make a mixed number, and simplify the fraction part.

items.q: Darnell has to cut a steel bar 4 3/8 feet long. His cutting chart counts eighths. How many eighths is that? 4 3/8 = ____/8
items.why: 4 wholes = 4 × 8 = 32 eighths. Add the 3 more: 32 + 3 = 35. 4 3/8 = 35/8.
items.no: Multiply the whole number by the denominator first (4 × 8), then add the numerator. The denominator stays 8.

notes.do: Hands off. He writes both steps for each one.
notes.ask: For the pipe, what improper fraction did you get first?
notes.listen: 26/8, which is 3 2/8 = 3 1/4. Watch for 3 2/8 (not simplified) and for 18/45 left unsimplified in the first one.

slides.title: Be the checker
slides.text: Each one has a mistake. Find it.

items.q: Nia wrote 2/5 = 3/6 because she added 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom. Is she right?
choices: Yes, because she changed both numbers the same way.
No. 3/6 is one half, but 2/5 is less than half.
No. She needed to add 2 to both numbers, not 1.
Yes, because both fractions are less than one whole.
items.why: 3/6 is exactly 1/2. Half of 5 is 2 1/2, so 2/5 is less than 1/2. Adding to both numbers changes the amount. A true equivalent: 2/5 × 2/2 = 4/10.
no: Changing both numbers the same way only works when you multiply or divide. Adding changed the amount: 3/6 is one half, and 2/5 is less.
Adding 2 gives 4/7, another different amount. Adding never makes an equivalent fraction.
Many fractions are less than 1 and still not equal. 3/6 is exactly one half, and 2/5 is less than half.

items.q: Marcus divided 20/36 by 2/2 and got 10/18. He says he is finished. What should he do?
choices: Nothing. 10/18 is already in simplest form.
Stop. 10/18 is fine because 18 is not prime.
Divide the top by 2 and the bottom by 3: 5/6.
Keep going. 10 and 18 share 2, so it is 5/9.
items.why: 10 and 18 are both even, so they still share 2: 10/18 = 5/9. The GCF of 20 and 36 is 4, and 20/36 ÷ 4/4 = 5/9 in one step. He used a common factor, but not the greatest one.
no: 10 and 18 are both even, so they share 2. It is not in simplest form.
Prime or not does not matter. 10 and 18 still share the factor 2.
Dividing the top and bottom by different numbers changes the amount. Use the same number for both.

items.q: Kofi changed 5 2/3 to the improper fraction 10/3. Which check proves he made a mistake?
choices: 10/3 = 3 1/3, and 3 1/3 is less than 5 2/3.
10/3 has a bigger numerator than 5 2/3 does.
The denominator should be 15, not 3.
10 is an even number, so it cannot be right.
items.why: Convert back: 10 ÷ 3 = 3 R1, so 10/3 = 3 1/3. That is less than 5 2/3, so 10/3 is wrong. He multiplied 5 × 2. The right way: 5 × 3 = 15 thirds, plus 2 more = 17/3.
no: Comparing the top numbers does not prove anything here. Convert 10/3 back to a mixed number and compare.
The denominator stays 3 when you convert. The mistake is in the numerator.
Even numbers can be numerators. Convert 10/3 back: it is only 3 1/3.

notes.do: He says which step went wrong and proves it: for the first, compare both to 1/2; for the last, convert 10/3 back (3 1/3).
notes.say: These are the three big fraction mistakes: adding instead of multiplying, stopping before simplest form, and multiplying by the wrong number when converting.
notes.ask: How can converting back catch Kofi's mistake?
notes.listen: 10 ÷ 3 = 3 R1 = 3 1/3, not 5 2/3. Checking backward catches it.

slides.title: Math check
slides.text: On your own. Paper first, then type.

items.q: Simplify in one step with the GCF: 32/48 = ____
items.no: Find the greatest common factor of the numerator and the denominator. Divide BOTH by it. Then check: do the new numbers share any factor except 1?

items.q: Mr. Nguyen joins 22 short pieces of pipe into one straight line. Every piece is 1/4 foot long. How long is the line? Type a mixed number in simplest form.
items.why: 22 pieces of 1/4 = 22/4 feet. 22 ÷ 4 = 5 R2, so 22/4 = 5 2/4. 2/4 simplifies to 1/2 (divide both by 2). 5 1/2 feet
items.no: Write it as an improper fraction first (22/4). Then divide to make a mixed number, and simplify the fraction part.

notes.do: Hands off. Note his first answers. Then switch to reading (10:05).
notes.listen: 2/3 and 5 1/2. Both right on the first try means he is ready for Pathways Week 12 Math (Saturday on his task list). Watch for 4/6 or 8/12 (stopped early) and 5 2/4.

slides.title: Reading words for today
slides.text: Tap each card. Read the word, the meaning and the example out loud.

words.meaning: Nonfiction writing whose job is to explain a real topic and give the reader true facts about it.
words.example: An article about how tower cranes work is informative writing.

words.meaning: The sentence that states what the whole paragraph is about. Writers usually put it first.
words.example: “A tower crane is the tallest tool on a building site” is a topic sentence.

words.meaning: A sentence that proves or explains the main idea with a fact, an example or a reason.
words.example: “Each morning, the operator climbs up inside the tower to the cab” is a supporting detail about the crane.

words.meaning: A connecting word or phrase, such as first, however or as a result, that shows how the next idea links to the one before.
words.example: “Next, the crew sets the window in place.” Next is a transition.

words.meaning: The final sentence of a paragraph. It says the main idea again with different words to close the paragraph.
words.example: “Careful steps like these keep every apartment dry” is a concluding sentence.

words.meaning: Not about the main idea, so it does not belong in the paragraph.
words.example: “The crane operator's favorite color is green” is off-topic in a paragraph about how cranes work.

notes.do: He reads each card aloud and covers it. Extra time on transition and concluding sentence: Pathways asks him to TYPE both.
notes.say: Now we switch to writing. Informative writing teaches facts. Each paragraph holds up one main idea, the way each floor of a building sits on the one below it.
notes.ask: How is informative writing different from the persuasive writing in Lesson 2?
notes.listen: Informative teaches facts; persuasive tries to change your mind. Have him spell transition and concluding out loud.

slides.title: Every sentence has a job
slides.text: Read the model paragraph. Each sentence does one job.

visual.text:
Laying a Tile Floor
A tile setter follows careful steps to lay a floor. First, he sweeps the floor and checks that it is flat. Next, he spreads a sticky layer called mortar and presses each tile into it. He also puts small plastic spacers between the tiles so the lines stay straight. When every tile is set, he fills the gaps with grout. These careful steps give the floor a smooth, even finish that lasts for years.

steps.text: Topic sentence (the foundation): it tells the main idea, and everything rests on it. “A tile setter follows careful steps to lay a floor.”
Supporting details (the floors): facts and examples that back up the main idea. Sweeping, mortar, spacers, grout.
Transitions (the stairs): First, Next, also, When every tile is set. They guide the reader from one step to the next.
Concluding sentence (the roof): it says the main idea again with different words. “These careful steps give the floor a smooth, even finish that lasts for years.”
Stay on one idea. Suppose the paragraph also said “Diego’s truck is blue.” That sentence would be off-topic, so the writer crosses it out.

slides.tip: Ask about every sentence: does it back up the topic sentence?

notes.do: He highlights the paragraph on paper (or points on screen): color 1 = topic sentence, color 2 = transitions, color 3 = concluding sentence.
notes.say: The concluding sentence says the main idea again, with different words. It does not add a new topic.
notes.ask: Which words in the concluding sentence connect back to the topic sentence?
notes.listen: “careful steps” and “floor.” It brings the reader back to the main idea.

slides.title: Transitions have jobs
slides.text: A transition tells the reader how the next idea connects to the one before it. Choose a transition by its job.

steps.text: Order: first, next, then, finally. “First, the crew measures the window opening. Next, they set the window in place.”
Example: for example. “Builders use many big machines. For example, a bulldozer pushes dirt into piles.”
Contrast (a difference): however. “Steel beams are very strong. However, they rust if they stay wet.”
Effect (a result): as a result. “The concrete truck was two hours late. As a result, the crew poured the floor after lunch.”
Add a detail: also. “The lobby gets new lights. It also gets a tall mirror.”
Comma rule: when a transition opens a sentence, a comma goes right after it: “Next, they set the window in place.” “However, they rust if they stay wet.”

slides.tip: Ask: how do the two ideas connect? Order, example, difference, result, or one more detail?

notes.do: Write the five jobs on the whiteboard as column headings. He adds one transition under each from memory.
notes.say: However is NOT just another detail. It means the next idea is different or surprising.
notes.ask: “Roofers nail shingles onto the roof. ____, landscapers plant trees by the front door.” Which transition fits?
notes.listen: Also (one more detail) or Next (the next job). However does not fit: planting trees is not the opposite of nailing shingles.

slides.title: The tallest tool on the site
slides.text: Read the article out loud. Highlight the transitions.

visual.text:
The Tallest Tool on the Site
(1) A tower crane is the tallest tool on a building site. (2) It arrives on trucks in pieces, and the crew bolts it together like a giant building set. (3) As the apartment building grows, the crew adds new sections to make the crane taller. (4) Each morning, the operator climbs up inside the tower to the cab, where the controls are.

(5) Wind is the biggest danger for a tower crane. (6) A small spinning tool on top of the crane measures how fast the wind is blowing. (7) My little brother loves to fly kites at the park. (8) When the wind gets too strong, the operator must stop lifting. (9) As a result, cranes often sit still on stormy days.

items.q: In the second paragraph, which sentence is the topic sentence?
choices: (6) A small spinning tool on top of the crane measures how fast the wind is blowing.
(5) Wind is the biggest danger for a tower crane.
(9) As a result, cranes often sit still on stormy days.
(8) When the wind gets too strong, the operator must stop lifting.
items.why: Every other sentence in the paragraph is about wind and the crane. Sentence 5 tells that main idea.
no: That is a supporting detail: one fact about measuring wind.
That is the last sentence. It shows a result of the wind.
That is a supporting detail about what the operator does.

items.q: Which sentence is off-topic? Type its number.
items.why: Sentence 7 is about a brother flying kites. It does not tell about tower cranes, so it is off-topic.
items.no: Find the sentence that is not about the crane.
items.hint: It is in the second paragraph.

items.q: Sentence 9 starts with a transition. Which transition shows the effect? Type it.
items.why: “As a result, cranes often sit still on stormy days.” Sitting still is the effect of strong wind.
items.no: Look at the first words of sentence 9.

notes.do: He reads aloud, highlights the transitions (As the apartment building grows, Each morning, When, As a result) and crosses out the off-topic sentence.
notes.ask: What is the topic sentence of the FIRST paragraph?
notes.listen: Sentence 1: a tower crane is the tallest tool on a building site. Everything in paragraph 1 is about the crane itself.

slides.title: Put the paragraph in order
slides.text: Amara's notes about putting in a window got mixed up. Tap the sentences in order: topic sentence first, then the steps, then the concluding sentence.
steps: Putting a window into a new apartment takes careful steps.
First, the crew measures the opening in the wall.
Next, they set the window in place and check that it is level.
Then, they seal every edge so rain cannot sneak in.
Finally, an inspector sprays the window with water to test for leaks.
Careful steps like these keep every apartment warm and dry.
slides.why: Topic sentence first. First, Next, Then and Finally put the details in order. The concluding sentence wraps it up.
slides.hint: Which sentence tells the main idea of all the others? Start there.

notes.do: He reads each sentence out loud as he taps it and names the transition.
notes.ask: How did you know which sentence came last?
notes.listen: It wraps up the main idea (careful steps) and has no step in it. Finally is the last STEP, not the conclusion.

slides.title: Does it belong?
slides.text: The topic is my jiu-jitsu class. Tap a sentence, then tap its job.

items.text: Jiu-jitsu class teaches me much more than how to wrestle.
items.why: It tells the main idea of the whole paragraph.
items.hint: Which sentence could the others all back up?

items.text: First, every student bows before stepping onto the mat.
items.why: A fact about class that backs up the main idea.
items.hint: Is it one step or fact about class?

items.text: Next, we warm up with rolls and stretches.
items.why: Another step in class: a supporting detail.
items.hint: Does it tell what happens in class?

items.text: For example, I learned to stay calm when someone pins me.
items.why: An example of what class teaches.

items.text: The grocery store near my house sells fresh bread.
items.why: It is about a grocery store, not about jiu-jitsu class.
items.hint: Is this about class at all?

items.text: Every class makes me stronger, calmer and more respectful.
items.why: It wraps up the main idea in new words.
items.hint: Does it sum up the whole paragraph?

items.text: Our car needs new tires before winter.
items.why: It has nothing to do with jiu-jitsu class.
items.hint: Does it have anything to do with class?

items.text: We also practice escapes with a partner.
items.why: One more fact about class. Also adds a detail.

slides.done: Topic sentence = the main idea. Details back it up. The concluding sentence wraps it up. Off-topic sentences come out.

notes.do: He sorts all eight and says WHY before each tap.
notes.ask: The bread sentence might be true. Why does it still not belong?
notes.listen: Being true is not enough. It has to back up THIS paragraph's main idea.

slides.title: Words from memory
slides.text: No word list. Type the answer.

items.q: Type the transition that fits: The paint was still wet. ____, nobody could hang pictures that day.
items.why: Nobody could hang pictures BECAUSE the paint was wet. That is an effect: As a result.
items.no: How are the two ideas connected? Is the second one an example, a difference, or a result?
items.hint: It is the transition for an effect.

items.q: Most paragraphs open with the ________ sentence, which states what the whole paragraph is about.
items.why: It is the topic sentence.
items.no: It usually comes first in the paragraph.

items.q: A paragraph closes with a ________ sentence that says its main idea again with different words.
items.why: It is the concluding sentence.
items.no: It concludes, or closes, the paragraph.

notes.do: No peeking at the vocab slides. A missed word is said three times, spelled out loud, then typed again.
notes.listen: Spelling counts on Pathways: t-o-p-i-c, c-o-n-c-l-u-d-i-n-g.

slides.title: Simplify, then convert
slides.text: 54/12 as a mixed number in simplest form

steps.text: 1. Find the GCF. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. 6 is a factor of 54 (6 × 9 = 54), and 12 is not. GCF = 6.
3. Convert. 9 ÷ 2 = 4 R1. 9/2 = 4 1/2. (Or convert first: 54/12 = 4 6/12, and 6/12 = 1/2. Same answer.)
Going the other way: 2 5/8 = 2 × 8 + 5 = 16 + 5 = 21 eighths. 2 5/8 = 21/8.

slides.tip: Equivalent: multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number. Simplify: divide by the GCF. Convert: divide, or whole × denominator + numerator.

slides.title: Equivalent fractions
slides.text: What was the number multiplied by? Do the same to the other number.

items.q: 7/8 = ____/40 Type the missing numerator.
items.why: 8 × 5 = 40, so multiply the numerator by 5 too: 7 × 5 = 35. 7/8 = 35/40.
items.no: What do you multiply 8 by to get 40? Multiply the numerator by that same number.

items.q: 3/7 = 27/____ Type the missing denominator.
items.why: 3 × 9 = 27, so multiply the denominator by 9 too: 7 × 9 = 63. 3/7 = 27/63.
items.no: This time the numerator changed. What do you multiply 3 by to get 27? Do the same to the denominator.

items.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 15/35?
no: That divides the top by 3 and the bottom by 5. Divide both by the SAME number.
That subtracts 1 from both. Subtracting changes the amount.
That divides the top by 5 and the bottom by 7. Divide both by the SAME number.

slides.title: Simplify it
slides.text: List the factors. Divide by the GCF.

items.q: Simplify in one step with the GCF: 27/45 = ____
items.no: Find the greatest common factor of the numerator and the denominator. Divide BOTH by it. Then check: do the new numbers share any factor except 1?

items.q: To simplify 40/56 in ONE step, divide the numerator and the denominator by ____.
items.no: Find the GREATEST factor that 40 and 56 share. 2 and 4 work, but they are not the greatest.

items.q: Which fraction can still be simplified?
items.why: 14 and 35 share the factor 7: 14/35 = 2/5. The others share no factor except 1.
no: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 and 15 = 3 × 5. Only 1 is common, so it is in simplest form.
9 = 3 × 3 and 20 = 2 × 2 × 5. Only 1 is common, so it is in simplest form.
11 and 12 share only 1. It is in simplest form.

slides.title: Convert it
slides.text: Type a mixed number with a space: 4 5/6.

items.q: Change it to a mixed number: 29/6 = ____
items.why: 29 ÷ 6 = 4 R5. The quotient 4 is the whole number. The remainder 5 is the new numerator, and the denominator stays 6. 4 5/6
items.no: Divide the numerator by the denominator. The quotient is the whole number, the remainder is the new numerator, and the denominator stays the same. Type a space between the whole number and the fraction.

items.q: Change it to an improper fraction: 7 3/4 = ____/4 Type the numerator.
items.why: 7 wholes = 7 × 4 = 28 fourths. Add the 3 more: 28 + 3 = 31. 7 3/4 = 31/4.
items.no: Multiply the whole number by the denominator first (7 × 4), then add the numerator. The denominator stays 4.

items.q: Which is 44/6 as a mixed number in simplest form?
items.why: 44 ÷ 6 = 7 R2, so 44/6 = 7 2/6. Simplify the fraction part: 2/6 = 1/3. 7 1/3
no: 7 2/6 is the right amount, but 2/6 is not in simplest form.
The quotient and the denominator got mixed up. 44 ÷ 6 = 7 R2, and the denominator stays 6 before you simplify.
2/6 is not 1/2. Divide 2 and 6 by 2: 1/3.

slides.title: Two-step jobs
slides.text: Underline what the question asks for.

items.q: A kitchen floor is covered with 64 tiles. 40 of them are blue, and every other tile is white. What fraction of the tiles are white? Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Step 1: 64 − 40 = 24 white tiles, so 24/64. Step 2: the GCF of 24 and 64 is 8. 24 ÷ 8 = 3 and 64 ÷ 8 = 8. 3/8
items.no: Two steps. First subtract to find how many are white. Then write that number over 64 and divide both by the GCF.

items.q: Mr. Nguyen joins 27 pieces of pipe into one straight line. Every piece is 1/6 foot long. How long is the line? Type a mixed number in simplest form.
items.why: 27 pieces of 1/6 = 27/6 feet. 27 ÷ 6 = 4 R3, so 27/6 = 4 3/6. 3/6 simplifies to 1/2 (divide both by 3). 4 1/2 feet
items.no: Write it as an improper fraction first (27/6). Then divide to make a mixed number, and simplify the fraction part.

items.q: A steel bar must be 5 2/3 feet long. Darnell's chart counts thirds. How many thirds is that? 5 2/3 = ____/3
items.why: 5 wholes = 5 × 3 = 15 thirds. Add the 2 more: 15 + 2 = 17. 5 2/3 = 17/3.
items.no: Multiply the whole number by the denominator first (5 × 3), then add the numerator. The denominator stays 3.

(1) An elevator is one of the last big machines put into a new building. (2) First, workers build a tall concrete tube called a shaft. (3) Next, they hang strong steel cables from a motor at the top. (4) However, nobody can ride the elevator until an inspector tests its brakes. (5) As a result, most elevators open only a few weeks before families move in.

teacher.objective: Math (35 min): Ethan shows with tile models that equivalent fractions name the same amount (3/8 = 6/16 = 9/24), finds a missing numerator or denominator by multiplying or dividing by n/n (and explains why adding to the top and bottom does not work), simplifies a fraction in one step by dividing by the greatest common factor from Lesson 6 and checks that the result is in simplest form, converts improper fractions to mixed numbers by dividing (the remainder becomes the numerator over the same denominator) and mixed numbers to improper fractions (whole × denominator + numerator), and solves Pathways-style two-step problems: the fraction of tiles that are the OTHER color in simplest form, and a line of unit-fraction pipes written as a mixed number in simplest form. Reading (25 min): he names the parts of an informative paragraph (topic sentence, supporting details, transitions, concluding sentence), matches transitions to their jobs (order, example, contrast, effect, add) with the comma rule, finds the topic sentence and the off-topic sentence in a two-paragraph article, puts a jumbled paragraph in order, and types the reading words from memory.
materials: The class lesson on a laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
Grid paper (Hallways A and B at 9:38: 8 boxes 2 squares wide, then 16 boxes 1 square wide; the 0-to-5 number line with 4 squares per foot at 9:49) and a blue colored pencil
Three highlighters or colored pencils (color 1 = topic sentence, color 2 = transitions, color 3 = concluding sentence; a pencil line through any off-topic sentence)
Whiteboard and marker (his hallway fractions at 9:30; factor pairs of 30 and 42 at 9:43; the five transition jobs at 10:12)
10 index cards (Word Power; he writes the words in class and finishes the meanings on Friday)
Pencil and paper; Packet (2 pages), printed: page 1 Friday, page 2 Sunday

plan.do: Class slides 1–2. He decides whether 3/8, 6/16 and 9/24 of a hallway are the same amount of floor. Write the three fractions on the whiteboard.
Class slide 3. GCF of 24 and 36 (Lesson 6), 2.4 × 3.5 (Lesson 4), 1/6 + 5/12 (Lesson 3), then 6/6 = 9/9 = 25/25 = 1.
Class slide 4. Improper fraction, simplify, convert, unit fraction. He writes each word on an index card.
Class slides 5–6. Hallways A and B on grid paper; × n/n and ÷ n/n; never add (3/8 vs 4/9). Then 4/9 = ?/36, 5/6 = 30/?, and the one fraction NOT equal to 6/10.
Class slides 7–8. 30/42 = 5/7: the slow way, then one step with the GCF (factor lists on the whiteboard). Then 24/32, the one-step divisor for 36/54, and which fraction is already simplest.
Class slides 9–10. 19/4 = 4 3/4 on a grid-paper number line; 3 5/6 = 23/6; 26/4 = 6 1/2. Then 27/5, 6 2/7 and 34/8.
Class slides 11–12. The 54-tile lobby (18/54 = 1/3 white) and 21 pipes of 1/6 foot (3 1/2 feet). Then 45 tiles with 27 gray, 26 pipes of 1/8 foot, and the 4 3/8-foot bar in eighths.
Class slide 13. Adding to top and bottom (2/5 = 3/6), stopping early (20/36 → 10/18), and 5 2/3 = 10/3. He proves each one.
Class slide 14 on his own: simplify 32/48 and the 22-piece pipe line. Note his first answers.
Class slide 15. Informative writing, topic sentence, supporting detail, transition, concluding sentence, off-topic. He spells transition and concluding out loud.
Class slide 16. The tile-floor model paragraph: color 1 topic sentence, color 2 transitions, color 3 concluding sentence. Foundation, floors, stairs, roof.
Class slide 17. Five jobs on the whiteboard (order, example, contrast, effect, add) and the comma rule. However is not “one more detail.”
Class slide 18. He reads aloud, highlights transitions, finds the topic sentence of paragraph 2, crosses out the off-topic sentence, and types As a result.
Class slide 19. Six window sentences in order: topic sentence, First, Next, Then, Finally, concluding sentence.
Class slide 20. Eight jiu-jitsu sentences into topic sentence, supporting detail, concluding sentence or off-topic. He says why before each tap.
Class slide 21. As a result, topic, concluding typed with no peeking.
Class slide 22. He says how to simplify 30/42 and convert 19/4. Open the course page and read the task list, then open the Winter Games page and read “What it is” together.

watch: Adding instead of multiplying: 3/8 → 4/9 or 5/6 = 30/31. Go back to the hallway strips: cutting every tile in 2 doubles BOTH numbers. Adding to both numbers always changes the amount.

Stopping before simplest form: 36/54 ÷ 9 = 4/6, or 20/36 → 10/18. He uses the GCF from his factor lists (Lesson 6) and then asks, “Do the new numbers share any factor except 1?” Pathways marks 6/8 wrong when it asks for simplest form.

Converting: the remainder goes over the SAME denominator (19/4 = 4 3/4, not 4 3/19), and for mixed → improper he multiplies the whole number by the DENOMINATOR (5 2/3 = 17/3, not 10/3). Checking backward catches both.

Typing mixed numbers: a space between the whole number and the fraction (4 3/4). Our lessons also accept 4-3/4 and 4 and 3/4; Pathways keeps the space and reads 43/4 as a different number. After converting, he simplifies the fraction part (3 2/8 → 3 1/4).
Two-step tile questions: they ask for the OTHER color (white, not blue). He underlines the color in the question before he subtracts. Forgetting step 1 gives the blue fraction.

Pathways Week 12 Math typed answers: missing-numerator questions accept the number or the full fraction (12 or 12/20); simplify questions need simplest form; it gives only 2 tries and only the first try earns points. Its math lesson also has a Fix the Sentence round (quotation marks from Lesson 6's dialogue, its vs. it's, commas in a series, subject-verb agreement): he retypes the sentence with the same words in the same order and fixes only capitals, punctuation or the one grammar mistake.

Transition jobs: however is a contrast, not “one more detail” (use also); as a result needs a real cause; for example needs a real example of the sentence before it. A comma goes right after a transition that starts a sentence.

Pathways Week 12 Reading: it reads a full article about the Houston build and asks for topic sentences, main ideas, the conclusion, which paragraph a new sentence belongs in, the off-topic sentence, and the best transition. Its Fix the Sentence round wants the exact sentence retyped (comma after the transition, capitals for names like Houston and Gulf of Mexico, verbs that agree, there/their, apostrophes). The Writer's Notebook paragraph earns XP only. Its Boss questions put four sentences in order using the topic sentence and transitions, which he practiced in class with different paragraphs.

packet_key.answer: topic sentence (concluding sentence is the extra choice)
Adding the same number to the top and bottom changes the amount (5/8 is more than 4/7); you must multiply or divide both by the same number. Any true equivalent, e.g. 8/14 or 12/21.
(2) First, (5) Finally, (However and As a result do not fit: nothing here is a contrast or an effect.)

Any 4 to 6 sentences on how to fold a paper airplane, with a topic sentence (for example, “Folding a paper airplane that flies far takes a few careful steps.”), at least two transitions with commas (First, Next, Then, Finally, For example, As a result), every sentence on topic, and a concluding sentence that wraps up the main idea in new words.

teacher.notes: For you only (do not share with Ethan): this lesson leans on Lesson 6: simplifying in one step needs the GCF, and converting uses his Lesson 2 division with a remainder. Before class, check his Lesson 6 Show What You Know score and his Pathways Week 11 scores: if Lesson 6 is under 85, spend the warm-up on factor pairs (24 and 36, then 30 and 42) and let him simplify in small steps first, then show the GCF shortcut; if Pathways Week 11 Math or Reading is under 85, add a retake to the Sunday line of his task list. Reading is a strength, so the reading block is short and practical: the parts of a paragraph, the job of each transition, and spotting the off-topic sentence, which is what Pathways Week 12 Reading scores. His weak spots are long multi-step procedures, TYPED answers and words from memory, so most items are typed, every conversion uses the same steps, and the 10 Word Power words go on index cards on Friday. All 10 words are new to him (none were used in Lessons 1 to 6). Finish: if both math exit-ticket problems are right on the first try, he is ready for Pathways Week 12 Math (Saturday on his task list, aim for 85). Pathways Week 12 Reading is on Thursday. Sunday is his retake day for either Pathways lesson under 85. The after-class lesson, Practice and Show What You Know use KCE paragraphs (Painting Day, Rooftop Gardens, Brick Walls, The Inspector's Visits, The Last Big Machine), not the Pathways article, and new numbers. Both Pathways lessons stop for a paper Pre-Lesson Warm-Up and a Post-Lesson Challenge; print them from the Pathways pre/post page if you want him to do the pencil breaks on paper. Tonight he does the after-class lesson (about 25 to 30 minutes, including Show What You Know): 10 questions (6 math and 4 reading; 3 different sets for retakes; he needs 85). The break: this is his last lesson of 2026. There is no class on Dec 23 or Dec 30, and you are away Dec 20–28. His task list runs Wednesday to Sunday and then hands him to The Ferguson Family Winter Games (Thu, Dec 17 – Tue, Jan 5). Its first days are short (family meeting Thursday, airplane workshop Friday, Games Day 1 Saturday, page 4 Sunday), so they sit next to this task list; his informative paragraph on Packet page 2 (how to fold a paper airplane) matches Friday's airplane workshop, and his Winter Games news report uses the same paragraph skills. Nothing on it needs you. The first January lesson is Wed, Jan 6: he presents his Winter Games Record Book (3 to 5 minutes). If he scores under 85 on Show What You Know, open the Formspree missed list at the start of the Jan 6 lesson: an adding mistake or a missing numerator means 5 minutes with the hallway strips; a fraction not in simplest form means factor lists and the GCF; a conversion mistake means the grid-paper number line and checking backward; a missed paragraph question means sorting sentences into topic, detail, conclusion and off-topic out loud; a missed word means index-card practice. The Winter Games Flight School Math Warm-Up (worksheet page 3) reviews fractions with mixed numbers and keeps the fall skills going.
